name: Apple
notes:
Fresh apples, nutrition from USDA. 90% is edible (core and stem removed).

World yield is FAO's average (~18 t/ha). The US gets about twice that (39.7 t/ha, USDA NASS 2019–2023). Water is the Mekonnen & Hoekstra footprint, lower in the US. Emissions are Poore & Nemecek's apple value (0.43 kg CO2e/kg), one of the lowest fruits.

Apples are sprayed often against scab, codling moth and other pests (captan, carbaryl, imidacloprid and others; ~5 kg/ha). The per-hectare figures for erosion, pesticides, fertilizer and CO2 capture are older estimates: their notes don't say where the numbers came from, so treat them as rough.
land_types_note: Grown in long-cleared temperate forest regions (China, Europe, US Northeast/Northwest).

name: Banana
notes:
Bananas, nutrition from USDA. Only 65% is edible (peel removed). FAO yield (~32 t/ha), Mekonnen & Hoekstra water, and Poore & Nemecek emissions (0.86 kg CO2e/kg, including tropical land-use change).

Bananas are grown in humid tropical lowlands, much of it former rainforest, which the Land Use sliders weigh heavily. Export plantations spray heavily (mancozeb fungicide against black sigatoka, paraquat, chlorpyrifos; ~7 kg/ha). The per-hectare erosion, pesticide, fertilizer and CO2-capture figures are older estimates without a documented derivation. Pineapple borrows banana's pesticide profile.
land_types_note: Humid tropical lowlands in Latin America, India and Southeast Asia, largely former rainforest.

name: Avocado
notes:
Avocados, nutrition from USDA. 75% is edible (skin and pit removed).

Avocados are thirsty and land-hungry: ~2,000 L of water per kg (Mekonnen & Hoekstra), with heavy irrigation in Chile, Peru and Mexico. Emissions (~2.5 kg CO2e/kg) are high for a fruit, driven by forest clearing for orchards in Michoacán, Mexico. The value is labelled as Poore & Nemecek's 'other tropical fruits' category, but that category isn't in the OWID dataset, so its exact basis is uncertain.

Soil erosion and CO2 capture have notes that don't match the field (copied emission notes), so treat them as rough estimates.
land_types_note: Mexico (Michoacán highland forest clearing) plus irrigated dry regions in Peru, Chile and California.

name: Coconut
notes:
Coconut meat, nutrition from USDA. Yield is FAO's average (5.6 t/ha of coconut meat equivalent), mostly Indonesia, the Philippines and India. Some plantations replaced mangrove and coastal wetland.

Several values here are weak. Water (2,500 L/kg) is an estimate, because Mekonnen & Hoekstra have little direct coconut data (confidence 2). Emissions (3.3 kg CO2e/kg) are an estimate from a broad tropical-fruit category, as Poore & Nemecek don't report coconut on its own. Erosion and CO2 capture carry notes copied from the emissions field. Coconut oil is derived from this entry.
land_types_note: Coastal humid tropics (Indonesia, Philippines, India); some plantations on former mangrove and coastal wetland.

name: Strawberries
notes:
Fresh strawberries, nutrition from USDA. 94% is edible (caps removed). World yield ~24 t/ha (FAOSTAT); the US gets ~57 t/ha on irrigated California coast. Emissions: Poore & Nemecek's 'Berries & Grapes' world value (1.53) and a US farm-gate study (1.83, California and Florida).

Strawberries are the most heavily sprayed crop in the dataset: ~267 kg of active ingredient per ha (USDA, CA + FL). 70–85% of that is soil fumigants (chloropicrin, 1,3-dichloropropene) injected before planting. Fumigants aren't in the pesticide toxicity table, so they add to pesticide weight but not to the modelled insect, bee and worm deaths. There's no world pesticide figure, so the world falls back to the US value, which probably overstates the world. California fields are also tilled ~13 times a year.

source.title: India Science & Technology — Papaya fertilizer dose (Coorg Honey Dew)
source.note: EDUCATED GUESS (confidence 1, not a measured value): Papaya — fertilizer_kg_ha: no survey data exists. Research recommendations conflict: India ~N 300 + P2O5 300 + K2O 300 = 900 kg/ha/yr (Tamil Nadu studies) or 250 g N + 250 g P2O5 + 500 g K2O per plant per year (Coorg Honey Dew, source 516); Brazil (Caliman 01, source 517) found the highest yield at N 1,088 + P 72 + K 527 and the best economic return at N 590 + P 72 + K 75 = 737 kg/ha. Trial rates run above what most farmers apply, so I took ~600 kg/ha, a bit below the Brazilian economic optimum (737) and well below the India figure (900). The previous banana stand-in (200 kg/ha) was far lower than any papaya recommendation I found.
